query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: A Bayesian optimization framework, trained on a minimal yet carefully selected set of high-temperature DSC and drop-calorimetry measurements for representative high-entropy alloy (HEA) compositions, will accurately and efficiently predict melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase heat capacities across the multi-principal-element composition space.
generation.material_initial_state: Near-equiatomic high-entropy alloys, typically single- or dual-phase FCC/BCC microstructures, prior to melting.
generation.intervention: Compile a sparse but strategically chosen experimental dataset using differential scanning calorimetry and drop calorimetry for various prototype HEA compositions, then apply Bayesian optimization to iteratively identify the next set of most informative compositions for measuring fusion-related properties.
generation.conditions: High-temperature characterization up to and across the alloy melting ranges, where reliable DSC and dilatometry or drop calorimetry is feasible.
generation.structural_mediator: Short-range chemical reconfigurations in the liquid phase, captured through thermodynamic descriptors, which guide the surrogate model in predicting property trends for novel compositions.
generation.mechanism: With each targeted new measurement, the Bayesian optimization updates the model parameters, refining predictive power for key melting properties by linking composition-structure to thermodynamic behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model will enable property predictions for Tm to within ~15 K, and for enthalpy/entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase heat capacities to within 5–10% of measured values for compositions covered by the training data.
generation.baseline: Previous CALPHAD-based high-throughput methods without adaptive sampling; existing partial property data from the literature and limited single-composition experiments.
generation.boundary: Applicable to HEAs whose composition–phase space remains within the calibration range of the optimization framework and for which accurate thermodynamic data exist. Predictions are less certain for highly complex or unexplored compositional extremes.
generation.uncertainty: Volume-change measurements near melting may show higher experimental variability. Data sparsity in new or unusual compositions can reduce model fidelity.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a broad set of newly formulated HEA compositions beyond the training range of the model. Perform DSC, drop calorimetry, and in-situ dilatometry measurements to obtain melting temperatures, enthalpies/entropies of fusion, volume changes, and liquid-phase heat capacities. Compare these experimental data to model predictions.
measurements: Melting onset and peak temperature from DSC
Integrals of DSC peaks for enthalpy and derived entropy of fusion
Volume change at melting using in-situ dilatometry or X-ray scattering
Liquid-phase heat capacity (Cp) via drop calorimetry over relevant temperature intervals
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If measured values systematically deviate from predicted values by more than 15% for multiple out-of-sample HEA compositions, the proposed Bayesian optimization approach is invalidated.

cited_evidence.text:
The concept of HEAs provides us an unprecedented degree of freedom in the design of advanced alloys with promising properties. For the rapid exploration of the vast compositional space and investigation of the composition and temperature effects on the microstructure, advanced HEA-design strategies and efficient tools are necessary. At present, a few advanced HEA-design strategies were reported by combining the physicochemical criteria, CALPHAD, data mining, and multi-objective optimization algorithm [21] , [22] , [35] – [37] , demonstrating that the CALPHAD method has played an important role in the design of advanced HEAs. There are two essential requirements to carry out calculations, using the CALPHAD method: computational software and database.

The computational software could significantly affect the efficiency of HTC since massive calculations are carried out. The CALPHAD approach [38] – [40] is currently the only method that can be used to obtain multicomponent phase diagrams with enough accuracy for practical applications without the need of the heavy experimental work [41] . This argument has made the CALPHAD method a key building block in the two largest driving forces in materials engineering today—ICME (Integrated computational materials engineering) [42] and MGI (Materials Genome Initiative) [43] . The application of the CALPHAD method requires both the thermodynamic database to provide the Gibbs energies (as a function of pressure, temperature, and composition) for the individual phases and the computational software to calculate the equilibrium state by an energy-minimization procedure. Over the past three decades, the development of consistent multicomponent thermodynamic databases has grown steadily, and several commercial software, such as Pandat TM [44] , Thermo-Calc [45] and FactSage [46] , has become available. decision.trend: Recent efforts to tackle the vast composition space of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) at high temperatures have relied on high-throughput computational screening (PMC8282813) and on advanced manufacturing routes for refractory HEAs (PMC9229239). In the computational screening approach, candidate compositions are sifted based on melting-point thresholds and predicted high-temperature stability, but the focus has been on solid-state strengthening phases rather than systematically quantifying Tm, enthalpy/entropy of fusion, or volume change at melting. Meanwhile, progress in manufacturing methods for refractory HEAs has focused on achieving near-full density and high strength at elevated temperatures but has not addressed a broad, efficient measurement framework for liquid-phase thermodynamic properties. As a result, there remains a critical gap in accurately and quickly determining fusion-related thermodynamic properties across diverse HEA compositions.
decision.unsolved: Despite identifying promising high-melt-temperature alloys through computational screening and fabricating advanced refractory HEAs, no widely validated, scalable method yet exists to measure or predict, in a more universal manner, the melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, volume changes at melting, and high-temperature liquid-phase properties across the full HEA compositional space. Limited empirical data and the difficulty of direct high-temperature measurements leave this challenge unresolved.
decision.lever: Deploy a Bayesian optimization framework trained on targeted high-temperature DSC and drop-calorimetry measurements for representative HEA compositions. The model will iteratively identify new chemistries for minimal additional experiments, thereby building a robust, predictive surrogate for Tm, enthalpy/entropy of fusion, volume changes, and liquid-phase heat capacities across the entire HEA range.
decision.why: High-throughput screening has shown promise (PMC8282813), but a direct, comprehensive approach for thermodynamic measurements is lacking. Machine learning with adaptive Bayesian sampling can exploit sparse but carefully chosen data to predict key transformation properties more broadly, addressing both accuracy and efficiency demands. A decisive validation would be to measure out-of-sample HEA compositions with the same high-temperature techniques and confirm alignment of predicted and measured fusion properties within a defined error margin. Failure to achieve quantitative agreement within that margin over multiple compositions would invalidate the model.
